questions.q: In this lesson's design, why is `caseStatusBadge` built and tested before `caseRow` and `caseDashboard`?
options: Because status badges are visually the most important part of the dashboard
Because caseStatusBadge must be deployed before any Apex class can be created
Because Jest tests can only be written for components with no @api properties
Because it's a leaf component with no dependencies on other new components, fitting a bottom-up build order where dependencies are built and tested before the components that compose them
questions.explain: caseStatusBadge has no dependency on the other new components, so it can be built and tested in isolation first -- then caseRow (which depends on it), and finally caseDashboard, which composes everything else.

questions.q: Why does this design use Lightning Message Service, rather than a custom event, to update a separate caseDetailPanel elsewhere on the page when a case is selected?
options: Because custom events are deprecated in current API versions
Because LMS is required for any component that uses NavigationMixin
Because caseDetailPanel is not a parent or child of caseRow/caseDashboard in the component tree -- LMS is the tool for components with no such relationship, exactly as covered in Lesson 12
Because custom events cannot carry a payload larger than one field
questions.explain: A plain custom event only reaches a listener attached directly to the dispatching element. Since caseDetailPanel has no parent-child relationship with the dashboard's components, LMS is the appropriate tool, matching Lesson 12's guidance exactly.

questions.q: Why is `filteredCases` designed as a getter rather than a field manually updated inside the filter-change handler?
options: A getter derived from the wired data and the current priorityFilter can never go stale, since there's no separate copy to remember to keep in sync -- consistent with Lesson 8's reasoning
Getters execute faster than any manually-managed field in every case
Fields cannot be filtered using JavaScript array methods
Only getters can be referenced inside a for:each directive
questions.explain: This directly applies Lesson 8's lesson on derived values: a getter recomputes fresh from its real inputs (the wired cases and priorityFilter), so it can't fall out of sync the way a manually-updated separate field could.

questions.q: Why does caseRow keep its `caseselect` event (for previewing) and its NavigationMixin-driven 'view' action (for navigating away) as two separate behaviors?
options: Because NavigationMixin cannot be combined with custom events in the same component
Because events must always fire before any navigation can occur
So that clicking the row to preview a case and clicking a dedicated icon to navigate to the full record don't trigger the same behavior, since they serve different user intents
Because @api properties cannot coexist with NavigationMixin in the same class
questions.explain: The row-click (preview via event) and icon-click (navigate away) serve genuinely different user intents, so the design deliberately keeps them as separate, independently triggerable actions rather than conflating them.

questions.q: Where in this design does an initial data-load failure surface to the user?
options: It is silently ignored, since wired Apex calls cannot fail
Only in the browser console, with no user-facing feedback at all
Through the error branch of the wired result, displayed as a ShowToastEvent with variant: 'error'
Through a dedicated errorPanel component not otherwise described in this design
questions.explain: The design explicitly routes a wire failure's error branch into a ShowToastEvent with an error variant, consistent with Lesson 21's pattern for surfacing failures to the user.
